title: Reading displacement-time and velocity-time graphs
learning_outcomes: Identify the quantity and unit shown on each axis of a motion graph.
Read displacement and velocity values, including positive, zero and negative values.
Translate sections of displacement-time and velocity-time graphs into descriptions of motion.
Recognise stationary motion, constant velocity, changing velocity and a reversal of direction.
Explain why a horizontal line has a different meaning on a displacement-time graph and on a velocity-time graph.
prior_knowledge_summary: From 9702_t02_cm01_l02, students know that positive and negative velocity show opposite directions in one-dimensional motion.
Students know that velocity may be zero, constant or changing.
Students know that acceleration describes a change in velocity, but they have not yet linked acceleration to a graph feature.
new_learning: Time is read from the horizontal axis and the named motion quantity is read from the vertical axis.
A displacement-time graph shows where an object is relative to a reference point as time passes.
A velocity-time graph shows the object's velocity directly as time passes.
On a displacement-time graph, a horizontal section means constant displacement and therefore stationary motion.
On a velocity-time graph, a horizontal section means constant velocity and only represents stationary motion when it lies on the time axis.
The sign of displacement gives the side of the reference point, while the sign of velocity gives the direction of motion.
A continuous velocity-time graph crossing the time axis shows a moment of rest and a change of direction.
not_yet_taught: Calculating or naming velocity as the gradient of a displacement-time graph
Calculating or naming acceleration as the gradient of a velocity-time graph
Drawing tangents or calculating graph gradients
Finding displacement or distance from area under a velocity-time graph
Constructing one motion graph from another using gradient or area

supporting_p1_demands: 9702_w20_11_q06 and 9702_w23_13_q05 distinguish cumulative distance from displacement and include stationary horizontal sections.
9702_w22_12_q06 links constant positive velocity with steadily increasing displacement.
9702_w24_11_q14 distinguishes zero velocity from zero acceleration at labelled points; this lesson uses only the zero-velocity motion state.
evidence_basis.scope_resolution: The mapped evidence reaches into later outcomes 9702_t02_m01_o03 and 9702_t02_m01_o05. This lesson uses only qualitative representation and motion-state interpretation under 9702_t02_m01_o02. No gradient or area relationship is taught or assessed.
evidence_basis.canonical_audit: Checked canonical questions and graph figures. 9702_w20_21_q02_a and 9702_w23_22_q01_c_i support graph reading/comparison.

excluded_mapped_parts.9702_m22_22_q02_a: Canonical part concerns zero horizontal force in projectile motion, not graph reading, so it is not used as question inspiration.

knowledge_boundary: This lesson reads coordinates, signs and qualitative shapes on displacement-time and velocity-time graphs. It does not calculate or name gradients, calculate areas, translate graphs by gradient or area, or use constant-acceleration equations.

blocks.title: The flat line that might still be moving
body: A tracking screen shows a perfectly horizontal line for five seconds.
Prediction: is the trolley definitely stationary?
It depends on the vertical axis. If the graph shows displacement, the trolley stays at one place. If it shows velocity at +3.0 m s^-1, the trolley keeps moving.
The same shape can tell two different stories. The axis label decides which story is true.

figure.purpose: Create the opening contradiction by showing identical horizontal shapes on two differently labelled motion graphs.
figure.brief: Hand-drawn split panel. Left: displacement against time with a horizontal line at +3 m. Right: velocity against time with a horizontal line at +3 m s^-1. Use identical line shapes and ask 'same motion?' without giving the answer in the image.
figure.alt_text: Two graphs have identical horizontal lines, but one has displacement on the vertical axis and the other has velocity.

blocks.title: Read the labels before the line
body: A graph is a record of two quantities. Time is on the horizontal axis. The quantity being tracked is on the vertical axis.
Before interpreting any line, name both quantities and their units.

Then read one point as a pair. At 4.0 s, a displacement coordinate of -2.0 m means the object is 2.0 m on the negative side of the reference point. At 4.0 s, a velocity coordinate of -2.0 m s^-1 means the object is moving in the negative direction.
blocks.remember: Axis first, coordinate second, motion story third.

blocks.title: A displacement-time graph is a moving position record
body: Imagine a trolley on a straight track with the start marked as displacement zero.
A point above the time axis places the trolley on the positive side of the start. A point below it places the trolley on the negative side.
If the line rises as time passes, displacement is becoming more positive, so the trolley moves in the positive direction.
If the line falls as time passes, displacement is becoming more negative, so the trolley moves in the negative direction.
A horizontal section means the displacement is unchanged. The trolley is stationary during that interval.

figure.purpose: Connect points on a displacement-time graph to actual trolley positions on a signed track.
figure.brief: Hand-drawn two-level representation. Top: signed straight track with origin and trolley positions at three times. Bottom: displacement-time graph with matching labelled points A, B and C. Show one increasing section and one horizontal section. Do not label gradient or velocity values.
figure.alt_text: Three trolley positions on a signed track match three points on a displacement-time graph, ending with constant displacement.

blocks.title: Mina walks past the reference point
body: Mina begins 4 m on the negative side of a lamp post. Her displacement-time line starts at -4 m.
The line rises, reaches zero and continues to +3 m. Mina moves in the positive direction, passes the lamp post and continues beyond it.
At displacement zero she is at the reference point. She is not necessarily stationary there.
Later the line becomes horizontal at +3 m. Only then does her position stop changing, so she is stationary.

figure.purpose: Separate being at displacement zero from being stationary.
figure.brief: Hand-drawn displacement-time graph for Mina. Start below the time axis, rise through zero to +3 m, then continue horizontally. Add a small lamp-post icon beside the zero-displacement level and label three times only. Do not add slope triangles.
figure.alt_text: Mina's displacement rises from negative through zero to positive, then stays constant at positive 3 metres.

blocks.title: A velocity-time graph reports motion directly
body: On a velocity-time graph, the vertical coordinate is the velocity itself.
A point above the time axis means positive velocity. A point below it means negative velocity. A point on the axis means zero velocity at that instant.
A horizontal line above or below the axis means constant velocity. The object is moving steadily, not resting.
A line that changes vertical position shows changing velocity. The velocity may change in size, sign, or both.

figure.purpose: Show how vertical position on a velocity-time graph directly encodes direction and rest.
figure.brief: Hand-drawn velocity-time graph divided into three consecutive intervals: constant positive velocity, changing velocity that reaches zero, and constant negative velocity. Add small direction arrows beside the intervals but no acceleration or gradient labels.
figure.alt_text: A velocity-time graph shows positive motion, a change to zero velocity, and then constant negative motion.

blocks.title: Think of each graph as answering a different question
body: For a displacement-time graph, ask: where is the object, and how does that position change next?
For a velocity-time graph, ask: which direction is it moving, and is the velocity staying the same?
A displacement of -5 m answers where. A velocity of -5 m s^-1 answers how it is moving.
This question-first method prevents the two vertical axes from being confused.

figure.purpose: Compare the meanings of coordinates and horizontal lines on the two graph types in one compact reference.
figure.brief: Hand-drawn comparison table with columns displacement-time and velocity-time. Rows: vertical coordinate, positive value, negative value, zero value, horizontal line. Keep cells short and include tiny graph icons with different vertical-axis labels.
figure.alt_text: A comparison table contrasts what coordinates, signs, zero and horizontal lines mean on displacement-time and velocity-time graphs.

blocks.title: Read a delivery robot's journey in stages
body: A velocity-time record begins with a horizontal line at +2 m s^-1. The robot moves steadily in the positive direction.
The line then moves down towards zero. Its positive velocity becomes smaller, so it is still moving in the positive direction but slowing down.
The line crosses zero and continues below the axis. At the crossing the robot is momentarily at rest. After the crossing it moves in the negative direction.
Finally the line is horizontal at -1 m s^-1. The robot now moves steadily in the negative direction.
No graph gradient or area is needed. We read the velocity coordinate and how it changes.

figure.purpose: Model a complete stage-by-stage reading of a velocity-time graph, including a reversal.
figure.brief: Hand-drawn velocity-time graph with four labelled stages A to D: horizontal at +2 m s^-1, descending while above axis, crossing zero, then horizontal at -1 m s^-1. Pair it with a simple four-frame robot direction sequence. Do not include shaded areas or slope triangles.
figure.alt_text: A robot has constant positive velocity, slows to zero, reverses, and then has constant negative velocity.

blocks.title: Why every horizontal line does not mean rest
body: It feels natural to think a flat line means nothing is happening. On many everyday displays, flat means unchanged, so the idea has a sensible origin.
The part that is unchanged depends on the vertical axis.
On a displacement-time graph, unchanged displacement means unchanged position, so the object is stationary.
On a velocity-time graph, unchanged velocity means steady motion. It is stationary only if that constant velocity is zero.
blocks.remember: Horizontal means the vertical quantity is constant. Always name that quantity.

blocks.title: A train waits, travels steadily and changes its motion
body: A displacement-time record is horizontal while a train waits at a platform. Its position does not change.
The record then rises steadily as the train moves in the positive direction at constant velocity.
Later the line still rises but its shape changes, so the train continues in the positive direction while its velocity changes.
At this lesson's level, describe these motion states. Lesson 4 will give a precise graph method for comparing velocities.

blocks.title: A five-step graph-reading routine
items: Name both axes and state their units.
Read the vertical coordinate at the stated time.
Use the sign according to the vertical quantity: side of reference point for displacement, direction of motion for velocity.
Decide whether the vertical quantity is constant or changing over the interval.
Translate the result into a complete motion sentence without using gradient or area.

blocks.title: One journey, two useful records
body: Displacement-time and velocity-time graphs can describe the same journey, but they do different jobs.
The displacement graph tracks position relative to a reference point. The velocity graph tracks direction and velocity directly.
Signs, zeros and horizontal sections only make sense after you identify the vertical axis.
That is enough to read a motion story before learning the calculation tools for graphs.

blocks.title: Return to the flat line
body: The flat line on the tracking screen was not enough evidence to say the trolley was stationary.
If displacement was constant, the trolley stayed in one place. If a non-zero velocity was constant, the trolley kept moving steadily.
Your mental model has changed from 'read the shape' to 'read the axes, then read the shape'.

requirements: Use only essential axes, units, points and motion cues.
Vary split-panel, spatial mapping, graph, comparison table and sequence forms.
Do not include gradient triangles, tangent lines, shaded areas or calculated graph quantities.
Do not reveal answers to any planned question figure.
Do not generate any image assets during this lesson-authoring pass.

concepts_taught: Motion graphs record time on the horizontal axis and a named motion quantity on the vertical axis.
Displacement-time graphs show position relative to a reference point as time passes.
Velocity-time graphs show velocity directly as time passes.
Signs, zero values and horizontal sections have meanings set by the vertical-axis quantity.
A continuous velocity-time graph crossing zero represents momentary rest and a change of direction.
Constant and changing motion can be described qualitatively from graph coordinates and shape.
misconceptions_addressed: Every horizontal motion-graph line means the object is stationary.
Displacement zero means the object is stationary.
Negative displacement means the object is moving in the negative direction.
A velocity-time graph crossing zero means the object has returned to its starting point.
skills_students_can_now_use: Identify and read motion-graph axes and units.
Read displacement or velocity at a stated time.
Describe stationary motion, constant velocity and changing velocity qualitatively.
Infer direction from displacement changes or from the sign of velocity.
Recognise a reversal from a continuous velocity-time graph crossing the time axis.
Distinguish the meaning of a horizontal line on displacement-time and velocity-time graphs.
next_lesson_can_assume: Students can distinguish displacement-time from velocity-time graphs by their axes.
Students can read coordinates, signs and qualitative changes on both graph types.
Students can describe constant and changing motion without calculating a gradient.
Students know the prior controlled concepts 9702_def_velocity, 9702_def_acceleration and 9702_formula_acceleration from earlier lessons.
next_lesson_must_not_assume: Gradient of a displacement-time graph gives velocity.
Gradient of a velocity-time graph gives acceleration.
A tangent gives an instantaneous gradient.
Area under a velocity-time graph gives displacement.
